title: Teachers of the year
hook: Job, Patacara, Julian, Frankl, Rabia, Kabir, Thérèse, Corrie ten Boom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus Aurelius, and your line was the surprise: the voice you didn't expect to learn from, thanked by name. Today the voices get faces, eight of them, lined up before the year ends. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

Who would you hire to teach a class on hard things? Probably not a man sitting among the ashes, scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery. Or a young mother wandering a road with nothing left. Or a woman so ill the people around her bed think she's dying. Or a prisoner in a camp, holding on to one reason to get through the night. As a faculty, it's a strange one. Nobody here has a corner office or a quiet life to teach from. And yet, when this year's questions got hard, these were the people who did the teaching. Today we call the roll one last time: eight teachers, and what each one left on the table.
screen: `THE ASHES. A ROAD. A SICKBED. A CAMP.` → `A STRANGE FACULTY.` → `EIGHT TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: First, the ones who grieved out loud. Job loses his children, his wealth and his health, and he won't accept his friends' tidy explanations. At the end of the book, God turns to those friends and says: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The one who argued is the one who spoke rightly. Patacara, as the Buddhist commentary tells it, loses her family and wanders out of her mind with grief. She meets the Buddha, comes back to herself, becomes a nun, and in time a teacher of others. Second, the ones who held on inside the pain. Julian of Norwich, in her showings, wondered why sin had not been prevented, and heard: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Viktor Frankl, writing after the camps, argued that one freedom can't be taken from a person: the freedom to choose an attitude. Neither of them pretended the pain was small. Third, the ones who loved and forgave without bargaining. Rabia of Basra, in a story people tell, walks with a torch and a bucket of water, to burn paradise and put out hell, so that God is loved for God alone. Kabir, in a verse kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that where there is forgiveness, there is God. Fourth, the ones who made it small and kept it hard. Thérèse of Lisieux called hers a little way: no great deeds, just the smallest things, done out of love. Corrie ten Boom, whose sister died in Ravensbrück, writes in The Hiding Place of a former guard holding out his hand, and of taking it. Eight teachers from many paths, and each one stays exactly who they are. None of them was asked to agree with the others.
screen: `JOB AND PATACARA: GRIEF, OUT LOUD.` · `JULIAN AND FRANKL: HOLDING ON INSIDE IT.` · `RABIA AND KABIR: NO BARGAINING.` · `THÉRÈSE AND CORRIE: SMALL, AND HARD.` · then, large: `MY TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a letter one line long. Pick one of the eight, or a teacher from this year who isn't on the list, or someone in your own life who taught you the same thing without a book. Settle first. Let the face, or the story, come into view. Then write one line to them, the way you'd write inside a card: what you took from them, or what you're still trying to learn. It doesn't need to be clever. If you pray, you can hold that teacher in prayer. If you don't, let the line rest on the page while you sit. The bell holds the time.
Patacara. One of this year's eight teachers, Job, Julian, Frankl, Rabia, Kabir, Thérèse and Corrie among them, people in hard places who did the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: my teachers. Keep the line you wrote somewhere you'll see it today, and when the moment fits, tell one person about the teacher it's for. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

howItsDone: People on many paths keep their teachers close by retelling their stories, reading their words, and remembering them by name; some write letters to teachers they never met as a way of saying what they learned.

myth: at the end of the book of Job, God sides with the friends who explained his suffering
God tells the friends they have not spoken rightly, as Job has (Job 42:7).
Rabia's torch and bucket comes from a verse of the Quran
it's a story people tell about her, not scripture.
Thérèse of Lisieux called her way a little way: the smallest things, done out of love
no great deeds; she made holiness small enough to fit an ordinary day.

fork.setup: you're one of Job's friends. he has lost everything, and he's angry at heaven. what do you do?
options: explain that his suffering must be punishment for something.
tell him to stop arguing with God.
stay with him, and let his complaint stand.
fork.reveal: the friends explained, and at the end of the book God says they had not spoken rightly, while Job, who argued, had.

original.note: Hebrew (Iyov): Job's name in the Hebrew Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: teachers are people who have the answers.
what it means: this year's teachers were mostly people in trouble: grieving, sick, imprisoned, arguing with heaven.
what a scholar hears: they reach us in different ways: Patacara through a commentary, Rabia through stories told about her, Julian, Thérèse and Corrie through their own books.

notes: Editor pass: hook no longer opens with a fragment list (days 1056 and 1061 use that shape), and the ash-heap line now follows Job 2:8 (sat among the ashes, scraped himself with a potsherd); Patacara framed as the commentary's telling, 'respected teacher' softened to 'a teacher of others'; Julian's question matched to chapter 27 (why sin was not prevented) and 'very ill' dropped from the teach; Kabir's forgiveness verse now sits under 'loved and forgave' rather than 'loved'.
Job 42:7 KJV quoted as a fragment; confirm wording.
Job scraping sores with a potsherd and sitting in ashes (Job 2:8) is used as an image in the hook; confirm it fits the KJV text.
Patacara summary follows the Therigatha commentary as the year-three outline gives it (loses her family, grief, meets the Buddha, becomes a nun and respected teacher); confirm.
Rabia's torch and bucket is presented as a story people tell, not a sourced text.
Kabir at Ang 1372 paraphrased (where there is forgiveness, there is God); confirm the Ang and the sense.
Corrie ten Boom: sister died in Ravensbrück; a former guard later offered his hand and she took it (The Hiding Place). Confirm the episode is in The Hiding Place rather than only in her later books.
Frankl described only as 'writing after the camps'; no dates or camp names given.
Original: אִיּוֹב (Iyov); confirm pointing and pronunciation guide.

Audit (2026-10-01): Thérèse's little way was summarized as 'small things done with great love', a phrasing widely attributed to Mother Teresa; now 'the smallest things, done out of love' (Story of a Soul, Manuscript B), in the teach and the myth. Patacara 'running' down a road changed to 'wandering' (the commentary has her wandering in grief).
